english_translation: Take the book on the table and give it to me so I can read for a bit.

dialogue.shona: Tora bhuku riri patafura undipe ndimboverenga.
dialogue.english: Take the book on the table and give it to me so I can read for a bit.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Tora [take! / pick up!] • bhuku [book] • riri [riri] • patafura [on the table] • undipe [undipe] • ndimboverenga [ndimboverenga]

grammar_notes.title: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('Tora')
grammar_notes.content: Notice the command verb 'Tora' in this sentence. In Shona, a direct command to one person (singular) is simply the verb stem ending in '-a'—for example, 'Vhara!' ('Close!'), 'Tora!' ('Take!'), or 'Huya!' ('Come!'). When speaking to more than one person, or when showing polite respect to an adult, you add '-i' to the end, changing '-a' to '-ai' (as in 'Huyai!' = 'Come!' or 'Batai!' = 'Catch/Hold!'). Adding the prefix 'chi-' (as in 'Chiuya' or 'Chigara') means 'Do it right now'.
grammar_notes.rule: Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('patafura')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'patafura'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Tora bhuku riri patafura undipe ndimboverenga.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

cultural_notes.title: Sharing Books & Reading Culture in Zimbabwean Homes
cultural_notes.content: Reading aloud and sharing books ('mabhuku') at the family table is a cherished part of home life in Zimbabwe, which consistently ranks among Africa's highest-literacy nations. Notice the softener '-mbo-' in 'ndimboverenga' ('so I can read for a little while'), which makes requests among family members sound warm and unhurried.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Baba vari mumba asi vana vari kutamba panze.'
options: Mother went to the market to buy fruit and vegetables.
The books and keys are lying on the table.
Father is in the house, but the children are playing outside.
We are going to the rural home tomorrow morning.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Father is in the house, but the children are playing outside.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Baba vari mumba' = 'Father is in the house', 'asi' = 'but', 'vana vari kutamba panze' = 'the children are playing outside'.

active_exercises.prompt: Which locative word means 'in the kitchen'?
Choose the natural English meaning of this new sentence: 'Vana vanoda kudya chingwa nemukaka mangwanani.'
options: The children want to eat bread and milk in the morning.
We bought sugar, salt, and vegetables yesterday.
Father is cooking meat and sadza for dinner tonight.
The bread has run out so I am going to the shop.
active_exercises.correct_answer: The children want to eat bread and milk in the morning.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vana' = 'The children', 'vanoda kudya' = 'want to eat', 'chingwa nemukaka' = 'bread and milk', 'mangwanani' = 'in the morning'.
